label: Generosity and Giving
framing: Generosity is not mainly a transfer of money but a loosening of the grip, the proof that you trust the Giver more than the gift. Scripture ties it to joy, calling God the lover of a cheerful giver, and treats the open hand as the surest cure for the quiet greed that hardens a heart.
cultural: In a world of scarcity and patronage, giving was usually a calculated move that put the receiver in your debt and raised your standing. Into that, Jesus told his followers to give in secret and to lend expecting nothing back, and the early church's lavish, unrepayable care for the poor broke every rule of ancient exchange, because it gave as those who had themselves received everything for free.
historical: The early Christians pooled their goods and fed the hungry, startling Rome with a generosity it could not explain. Basil of Caesarea in the fourth century told the rich that the coat in their closet belonged to the naked, and John Wesley in the eighteenth century, as his income rose, kept his spending fixed and gave the rest away, dying with little, having gained all he could only to give all he could.
application: Give first, off the top, before the rest of your spending bends around it, and you will find the fear loosen its grip. Decide your giving on purpose rather than by what is left over, and let it cost you something, since a gift that costs nothing changes nothing. Practice hospitality, the generosity of the table, and remember that you cannot outgive the God who gave his Son.

verses.text: One gives freely, yet gains even more; another withholds what is right, only to become poor. A generous soul will prosper, and he who refreshes others will himself be refreshed.
verses.where: One gives freely and gains even more; another withholds and becomes poor; the one who refreshes others is refreshed. The site's note on the chapter says generosity that seems to lose ends up gaining, and hoarding that seems to gain ends up cursed. The proverb describes how God's world tends to work, not a scheme for profit.

verses.text: In everything, I showed you that by this kind of hard work we must help the weak, remembering the words of the Lord Jesus Himself: ‘It is more blessed to give than to receive.’”
verses.where: Saying farewell to the Ephesian elders, Paul reminds them that he worked with his own hands to help the weak, remembering the Lord's words that it is more blessed to give than to receive. The site's plain note calls this Paul's last lesson, his own hands used for the weak, and asks whether you believe it, really, in your spending and your time. Giving is called a blessing before it is called a duty.

verses.text: For I testify that they gave according to their ability and even beyond it. Of their own accord, they earnestly pleaded with us for the privilege of sharing in this service to the saints. And not only did they do as we expected, but they gave themselves first to the Lord and then to us, because it was the will of God.
verses.where: Paul tells of the Macedonian churches, who in deep poverty gave beyond their ability and begged to share in the gift for the believers in Jerusalem. The site's plain note says they gave themselves first to the Lord, and asks whether your money follows where your heart has already gone, or is the one thing you have kept back. It asks what would make giving feel like a privilege rather than a loss.

verses.text: For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though He was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor, so that you through His poverty might become rich.
verses.where: Paul grounds his appeal in Christ, who though rich became poor for their sake, so that through his poverty they might become rich. The site's plain note says the riches he gives are not money but forgiveness, a place in God's family, the Spirit and a future with God, and that Paul does not order the Corinthians to give but reminds them of Jesus. Christian generosity begins from what has already been given.

verses.text: If anyone with earthly possessions sees his brother in need, but withholds his compassion from him, how can the love of God abide in him? Little children, let us love not in word and speech, but in action and truth.
verses.where: John asks how God's love can abide in anyone who sees a brother in need and closes his heart, and calls for love in action and truth. The site's plain note asks whom you know in need right now and whether your love costs you anything. It adds that this is love freely given, not letting someone take from you by force or fear.

verses.text: Kindness to the poor is a loan to the LORD, and He will repay the lender.
verses.where: Kindness to the poor is a loan to the LORD, and he will repay the lender. The site's note on the Hebrew word for lend says the borrower is elsewhere the weaker party, which makes the verse remarkable: God places himself in the borrower's position on behalf of the poor. A gift to the poor is never lost in God's accounts.

verses.text: But when you give to the needy, do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing, so that your giving may be in secret. And your Father, who sees what is done in secret, will reward you.
verses.where: Jesus tells his followers to give so quietly that the left hand does not know what the right is doing, for the Father sees in secret. The site's note says he assumes they will give and attacks only the advertising of it, so that the poor are not turned into props for the giver's reputation. The plain note says the reward is not payment but the Father's notice of what no one else sees.

verses.text: When you reap the harvest of your land, you are not to reap to the very edges of your field or gather the gleanings of your harvest. You must not strip your vineyard bare or gather its fallen grapes. Leave them for the poor and the foreigner. I am the LORD your God.
verses.where: Israel is told not to reap to the edges of the field or strip the vineyard bare, but to leave the gleanings for the poor and the foreigner, ending with I am the LORD your God. The site's note on the chapter says every command is grounded in God's own character, with love of neighbour at the centre. Generosity was built into the way the harvest itself was done.

verses.text: But when you host a banquet, invite the poor, the crippled, the lame, and the blind, and you will be blessed. Since they cannot repay you, you will be repaid at the resurrection of the righteous.”
verses.where: Jesus tells his host to invite the poor, the crippled, the lame and the blind, who cannot repay. The site's note says the danger he names is not that the host will lose money but that he will be repaid, since generosity that expects a return is a transaction. The plain note says Jesus means real meals, and that a table which only ever holds people who can pay us back is too small.

verses.text: In Joppa there was a disciple named Tabitha (which is translated as Dorcas), who was always occupied with works of kindness and charity.
verses.where: In Joppa there was a disciple named Tabitha, always occupied with works of kindness and charity, and the widows show the tunics she made for them. The site's plain note says she is remembered by what she made for others, and that small, faithful kindness is not small to God. Generosity in Acts is often a needle and thread.

misread.taken: Whoever sows generously will also reap generously is used to promise that money given to God, or to a particular ministry, will come back many times over.
misread.says: The site's plain note says no, plainly: Paul says God will give all that you need, not all that you want; the harvest he names is the harvest of your righteousness, goodness and not goods; and the riches are to be generous on every occasion, so that people thank God. The people in these chapters who give most freely are poor and stay poor, and the note on the chapter says the return on generosity is the capacity for more generosity, not personal wealth. If you gave because someone promised God would pay you back, the plain note says, that was not your failure; the promise was wrong.
misread.text: Remember this: Whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and whoever sows generously will also reap generously.

whole: Most people want to be generous and find it harder than they expected. The bills come first, then the savings, then whatever is left, and there rarely is much left. Some give out of guilt or pressure and feel resentful afterwards. Some give and want it noticed. Some have been burned by appeals that promised a return or by charities that misused the gift, and have stopped giving at all. Others give money easily but not time, or time but not money. And some who have very little give more freely than those who have much, and do not think of it as anything special.

Scripture names what holds the hand closed. Proverbs sets the one who withholds beside the one who gives freely, and John asks how God's love can live in someone who sees a brother in need and shuts his heart. Jesus warns against giving to be seen, which turns the poor into props for a reputation, and against the generosity that is really a transaction, inviting only those who can invite you back. Beneath all of these lies fear, that there will not be enough, and the wish to stay in control of who owes what. Every one of us has felt the hand close at the wrong moment.

So the Bible's wisdom builds generosity into ordinary life. Israel left the edges of the field for the poor, so that giving was part of how the harvest was done. Paul told the Corinthians to give regularly and in proportion, and the Macedonians gave themselves first to the Lord and then their money. Jesus asks for quiet gifts the left hand does not know about, and for tables with guests who cannot repay. Tabitha's generosity was tunics, and Paul's was the work of his own hands for the weak. Give on purpose, cheerfully and not under pressure, and never because someone promised you a return.

The hope Scripture gives begins with a gift already made. Christ, though rich, became poor for our sake, and Paul does not order the Corinthians to give; he reminds them of Jesus. Kindness to the poor is a loan to the LORD, who places himself in the borrower's seat. Those who refresh others are refreshed, not with a payout but with the joy Paul remembered in Jesus' words: it is more blessed to give than to receive.
deep.sit: Who is in need near you right now, and what do you have that could help them this week?

prayer.lead: The site's plain note says generosity in this psalm is part of what it means to fear the LORD, and asks whether what you have is open-handed, like seed scattered on a field. It adds that the psalm describes how God's world tends to work, not a promise of riches.
prayer.text: It is well with the man who is generous and lends freely, whose affairs are guided by justice. Surely he will never be shaken; the righteous man will be remembered forever. He does not fear bad news; his heart is steadfast, trusting in the LORD. His heart is assured; he does not fear, until he looks in triumph on his foes. He has scattered abroad his gifts to the poor; his righteousness endures forever; his horn will be lifted high in honor.
